newsitem.title: BELGIUM: TRACTEBEL TAKES FOREIGN EXPANSION IN OWN HANDS.
newsitem.headline: TRACTEBEL TAKES FOREIGN EXPANSION IN OWN HANDS.

text.p: Belgian utility holding company Tractebel SA took its foreign expansion drive in its own hands on Thursday, sealing a merger with its Powerfin unit which had spearheaded that ambition.

At extraordinary assemblies of the two firms, shareholders overwhelmingly approved the merger, creating an international giant in electricity and gas services with a 255 billion ($7.27 billion) franc stock market capitalisation.
"Powerfin did not have the operational experience nor the size to win foreign contracts which Tractebel will be able to get," Tractebel chief executive officer Philippe Bodson said.
For the ebullient, confrontational, and sometimes controversial Bodson, the merger marks a personal triumph.

Bodson, who was CEO of Belgian glass producer Glaverbel before taking the helm at Tractebel in 1989, has turned a staid domestic energy group into a sharp international utilities player with electricity plants in 17 countries.

After just one year at Tractebel, Bodson in 1990 pushed through a merger of Belgium's three operational electricity companies to create Electrabel , which has a virtual monopoly on electricity production in Belgium.
A year later, Bodson announced that he wanted to go back to the roots of the company -- production abroad.
At the end of the 19th century, what is now known as Tractebel but what was then a myriad of companies built tramways around the globe, in China, Africa, Russia and South America.
From the electric tramways, Belgian engineers branched out into electricity production for regional authorities.

But the Russian revolution in 1917, World Wars One and Two, the Communist takeover in China and a series of nationalisations in a decolonised Africa left virtualy nothing of that once sprawling foreign empire.
Enter Bodson, who boldly announced that by the year 2000 he wanted the Tractebel group to produce as much electricity abroad as it produced in Belgium .
To the amazement of a once-sceptical analysts community, half a decade later proof is here that Bodson actually did create something out of nothing.

Of the 23,000 megawatts of electricity production capacity in hands of the Tractebel group today, 10,000 megawatts is abroad at plants in Argentina, Canada, Chile, Germany, Hungary, India, Italy, Kazakhstan, Northern Ireland, Oman, Peru, Portugal, Singapore, Thailand, the U.S. and Vietnam.

"Five years ago, Bodson's plans looked very ambitious indeed. But it must be said that Bodson, even if his outspokenness sometimes upsets people, is an excellent manager who is in the process of fulfilling his promise," said Bruno du Bus, an analyst with Brussels brokerage Puilaetco.
At Tractebel's annual shareholders meeting on Wednesday, Bodson said that he may reach his self-set target early.
"The achievements of the past five years strengthens my belief our target will be met before the year 2000," he said.
Bodson has, however, some new challenges ahead.
Compagnie de Suez , the French parent company of Tractebel's Belgian parent Societe Generale de Belgique, has merged with French utility group Lyonnaise des Eaux, formerly a Tractebel rival.
This has led to fears that Tractebel's expansion would become subordinate to those of its French masters.

At the shareholders meeting Wednesday, Gerald Mestrallet, head of the new Suez-Lyonnaise group, said Tractebel would remain separate, pursuing its own growth in electricity and gas, while the French group stays focussed on water services.
But both groups also have common activities, such as waste management, and could eventually compete for foreign contracts.
"We will see what happens then. This saga is not over yet," one analyst said.
